entries.78c96babd8dc6f1d6b1819cebac09abb82b10d05: <div sID="gen3876" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="29" osisID="Deut.29" sID="Deut.29"/> <div eID="gen3876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3877" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen3878" type="x-p"/> The first words of this chapter are the contents of it, "These are the words of the covenant" (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.1">ver. 1</reference>), that is, these that follow. Here is, I. A recital of God's dealings with them, in order to the bringing of them into this covenant, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.2-Deut.29.8">ver. 2-8</reference>. II. A solemn charge to them to keep the covenant, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.9">ver. 9</reference>. III. An abstract of the covenant itself, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.12-Deut.29.13">ver. 12, 13</reference>. IV. A specification of the persons taken into the covenant, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.10-Deut.29.11">ver. 10, 11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.14">14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.15">15</reference>. V. An intimation of the great design of this covenant against idolatry, in a parenthesis, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.16-Deut.29.17">ver. 16, 17</reference>. VI. A most solemn and dreadful denunciation of the wrath of God against such persons as promise themselves peace in a sinful way, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.18-Deut.29.28">ver. 18-28</reference>. VII. The conclusion of this treaty, with a distinction between things secret and things revealed, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.29">ver. 29</reference>.
entries.02d44ec91b78e00e411debc032782b58e39bd246: <div eID="gen3878" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen3877" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Mercies Called to Remembrance. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3879" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> These <hi type="italic">are</hi> the words of the covenant, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> commanded Moses to make with the children of Israel in the land of Moab, beside the covenant which he made with them in Horeb. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Moses called unto all Israel, and said unto them, Ye have seen all that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> did before your eyes in the land of Egypt unto Pharaoh, and unto all his servants, and unto all his land; <hi type="super">3</hi> The great temptations which thine eyes have seen, the signs, and those great miracles: <hi type="super">4</hi> Yet the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath not given you a heart to perceive, and eyes to see, and ears to hear, unto this day. <hi type="super">5</hi> And I have led you forty years in the wilderness: your clothes are not waxen old upon you, and thy shoe is not waxen old upon thy foot. <hi type="super">6</hi> Ye have not eaten bread, neither have ye drunk wine or strong drink: that ye might know that I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God. <hi type="super">7</hi> And when ye came unto this place, Sihon the king of Heshbon, and Og the king of Bashan, came out against us unto battle, and we smote them: <hi type="super">8</hi> And we took their land, and gave it for an inheritance unto the Reubenites, and to the Gadites, and to the half tribe of Manasseh. 9 Keep therefore the words of this covenant, and do them, that ye may prosper in all that ye do. <div eID="gen3879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3880" type="x-p"/> Now that Moses had largely repeated the commands which the people were to observe as their part of the covenant, and the promises and threatenings which God would make good (according as they behaved themselves) as part of the covenant, the whole is here summed up in a federal transaction. The covenant formerly made is here renewed, and Moses, who was before, is still, the mediator of it (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord commanded Moses to make it.</hi> Moses himself, though king in Jeshurun, could not make the covenant any otherwise than as God gave him instructions. It does not lie in the power of ministers to fix the terms of the covenant; they are only to dispense the seals of it. This is said to be <hi type="italic">besides the covenant made in Horeb;</hi> for, though the covenant was the same, yet it was a new promulgation and ratification of it. It is probable that some now living, though not of age to be mustered, were of age to consent for themselves to the covenant made at Horeb, and yet it is here renewed. Note, Those that have solemnly covenanted with God should take all opportunities to do it again, as those that like their choice too well to change. But the far greater part were a new generation, and therefore the covenant must be made afresh with them, for it is fit that the covenant should be renewed to the children of the covenant. <div eID="gen3880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3881" type="x-p"/> I. It is usual for indentures to begin with a recital; this does so, with a rehearsal of the great things God had done for them, 1. As an encouragement to them to believe that God would indeed be to them a God, for he would not have done so much for them if he had not designed more, to which all he had hitherto done was but a preface (as it were) or introduction; nay, he had shown himself a God in what he had hitherto done for them, which might raise their expectations of something great and answering the vast extent and compass of that pregnant promise, that God would be to them a God. 2. As an engagement upon them to be to him an obedient people, in consideration of what he had done for them. <div eID="gen3881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3882" type="x-p"/> II. For the proof of what he here advances he appeals to their own eyes (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">You have seen all that the Lord did.</hi> Their own senses were incontestable evidence of the matter of fact, that God had done great things for them; and then their own reason was a no less competent judge of the equity of his inference from it: <hi type="italic">Keep therefore the words of this covenant,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.29.9">v. 9</reference>. <div eID="gen3882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3883" type="x-p"/> III. These things he specifies, to show the power and goodness of God in his appearances for them. 1. Their deliverance out of Egypt, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.2-Deut.29.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. The amazing signs and miracles by which Pharaoh was plagued and compelled to dismiss them, and Israel was tried (for they are called <hi type="italic">temptations</hi>) whether they would trust God to secure them from, and save them by, those plagues. 2. Their conduct through the wilderness for forty years, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.5-Deut.29.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. There they were led, and clad, and fed, by miracles; though the paths of the wilderness were not only unknown but untrodden, yet God kept them from being lost there; and (as bishop Patrick observes) those very shoes which by the appointment of God they put on in Egypt, at the passover, when the were ready to march (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.11">Exod. xii. 11</reference>), never wore out, but served them to Canaan: and though they lived not upon bread which strengthens the heart, and wine which rejoices it, but upon manna and rock-water, yet they were men of strength and courage, mighty men, and able to go forth to war. By these miracles they were made to know that the Lord was God, and by these mercies that he was their God. 3. The victory they had lately obtained of Sihon and Og, and that good land which they had taken possession of, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.7-Deut.29.8">v. 7, 8</reference>. Both former mercies and fresh mercies should be improved by us as inducements to obedience. <div eID="gen3883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3884" type="x-p"/> IV. By way of inference from these memoirs, <div eID="gen3884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3885" type="x-p"/> 1. Moses laments their stupidity: <hi type="italic">Yet the Lord has not given you a heart to perceive,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.29.4">v. 4</reference>. This does not lay the blame of their senselessness, and sottishness, and unbelief, upon God, as if they had stood ready to receive his grace and had begged for it, but he had denied them; no, but it fastens the guilt upon themselves. "The Lord, who is the Father of spirits, a God in covenant with you, and who had always been so rich in mercy to you, no doubt would have crowned all his other gifts with this, he would have given you a heart to perceive and eyes to see if you had not by your own frowardness and perverseness frustrated his kind intentions, and received his grace in vain." Note, (1.) The hearing ear, the seeing eye, and the understanding heart, are the gift of God. All that have them have them from him. (2.) God gives not only food and raiment, but wealth and large possessions, to many to whom he does not give grace. Many enjoy the gifts who have not hearts to perceive the giver, nor the true intention and use of the gifts. (3.) God's readiness to do us good in other things is a plain evidence that if we have not grace, that best of gifts, it is our own fault and not his; he would have gathered us and we would not. <div eID="gen3885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3886" type="x-p"/> 2. Moses charges them to be obedient: <hi type="italic">Keep therefore, and do,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.29.9">v. 9</reference>. Note, We are bound in gratitude and interest, as well as duty and faithfulness, to <hi type="italic">keep the words of the covenant.</hi>
entries.8e3683094009bf36538ab118a0a0a52bf83ed4e1: <div eID="gen3886" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Covenant Renewed. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1451.)</title> <div sID="gen3887" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Ye stand this day all of you before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God; your captains of your tribes, your elders, and your officers, <hi type="italic">with</hi> all the men of Israel, <hi type="super">11</hi> Your little ones, your wives, and thy stranger that <hi type="italic">is</hi> in thy camp, from the hewer of thy wood unto the drawer of thy water: <hi type="super">12</hi> That thou shouldest enter into covenant with the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, and into his oath, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God maketh with thee this day: <hi type="super">13</hi> That he may establish thee to day for a people unto himself, and <hi type="italic">that</hi> he may be unto thee a God, as he hath said unto thee, and as he hath sworn unto thy fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. <hi type="super">14</hi> Neither with you only do I make this covenant and this oath; <hi type="super">15</hi> But with <hi type="italic">him</hi> that standeth here with us this day before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God, and also with <hi type="italic">him</hi> that <hi type="italic">is</hi> not here with us this day: <hi type="super">16</hi> (For ye know how we have dwelt in the land of Egypt; and how we came through the nations which ye passed by; <hi type="super">17</hi> And ye have seen their abominations, and their idols, wood and stone, silver and gold, which <hi type="italic">were</hi> among them:) <hi type="super">18</hi> Lest there should be among you man, or woman, or family, or tribe, whose heart turneth away this day from the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God, to go <hi type="italic">and</hi> serve the gods of these nations; lest there should be among you a root that beareth gall and wormwood; <hi type="super">19</hi> And it come to pass, when he heareth the words of this curse, that he bless himself in his heart, saying, I shall have peace, though I walk in the imagination of mine heart, to add drunkenness to thirst: <hi type="super">20</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will not spare him, but then the anger of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> and his jealousy shall smoke against that man, and all the curses that are written in this book shall lie upon him, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall blot out his name from under heaven. <hi type="super">21</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall separate him unto evil out of all the tribes of Israel, according to all the curses of the covenant that are written in this book of the law: <hi type="super">22</hi> So that the generation to come of your children that shall rise up after you, and the stranger that shall come from a far land, shall say, when they see the plagues of that land, and the sicknesses which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath laid upon it; 23 <hi type="italic">And that</hi> the whole land thereof <hi type="italic">is</hi> brimstone, and salt, <hi type="italic">and</hi> burning, <hi type="italic">that</hi> it is not sown, nor beareth, nor any grass groweth therein, like the overthrow of Sodom, and Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboim, which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> overthrew in his anger, and in his wrath: 24 Even all nations shall say, Wherefore hath the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> done thus unto this land? what <hi type="italic">meaneth</hi> the heat of this great anger? <hi type="super">25</hi> Then men shall say, Because they have forsaken the covenant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of their fathers, which he made with them when he brought them forth out of the land of Egypt: 26 For they went and served other gods, and worshipped them, gods whom they knew not, and <hi type="italic">whom</hi> he had not given unto them: <hi type="super">27</hi> And the anger of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> was kindled against this land, to bring upon it all the curses that are written in this book: <hi type="super">28</hi> And the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> rooted them out of their land in anger, and in wrath, and in great indignation, and cast them into another land, as <hi type="italic">it is</hi> this day. <hi type="super">29</hi> The secret <hi type="italic">things belong</hi> unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God: but those <hi type="italic">things which are</hi> revealed <hi type="italic">belong</hi> unto us and to our children for ever, that <hi type="italic">we</hi> may do all the words of this law. <div eID="gen3887" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3888" type="x-p"/> It appears by the length of the sentences here, and by the copiousness and pungency of the expressions, that Moses, now that he was drawing near to the close of his discourse, was very warm and zealous, and very desirous to impress what he said upon the minds of this unthinking people. To bind them the faster to God and duty, he here, with great solemnity of expression (to make up the want of the external ceremony that was used (<reference osisRef="Exod.24.4-Exod.24.8">Exod. xxiv. 4</reference>, &c.), concludes a bargain (as it were) between them and God, an everlasting covenant, which God would not forget and they must not. He requires not their explicit consent, but lays the matter plainly before them, and then leaves it between God and their own consciences. Observe, <div eID="gen3888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3889" type="x-p"/> I. The parties to this covenant. 1. It is the Lord their God they are to covenant with, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.12">v. 12</reference>. To him they must give up themselves, to him they must join themselves. "It is his oath; he has drawn up the covenant and settled it; he requires your consent to it; he has sworn to you and to him you must be sworn." This requires us to be sincere and serious, humble and reverent, in our covenant-transactions with God, remembering how great a God he is with whom we are covenanting, who has a perfect knowledge of us and an absolute dominion over us. 2. They are all to be taken into covenant with him. They were all summoned to attend (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.2">v. 2</reference>), and did accordingly, and are told (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.10">v. 10</reference>) what was the design of their appearing before God now in a body—they were to enter into covenant with him. (1.) Even their great men, the captains of their tribes, their elders and officers, must not think it any disparagement to their honour, or any diminution of their power, to put their necks under the yoke of this covenant, and to draw in it. They must rather enter into the covenant first, to set a good example to their inferiors. (2.) Not the men only, but their wives and children, must come into this covenant; though they were not numbered and mustered, yet they must be <hi type="italic">joined to the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.29.11">v. 11</reference>. Observe, Even little ones are capable of being taken into covenant with God, and are to be admitted with their parents. Little children, so little as to be carried in arms, must be brought to Christ, and shall be blessed by him, for <hi type="italic">of such</hi> was and <hi type="italic">is the kingdom of God.</hi> (3.) Not the men of Israel only, but the stranger that was in their camp, provided he was so far proselyted to their religion as to renounce all false gods, was taken into this covenant with the God of Israel, forasmuch as he also, though a stranger, was to be looked upon in this matter as a <hi type="italic">son of Abraham,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.19.9">Luke xix. 9</reference>. This was an early indication of favour to the Gentiles, and of the kindness God had in store for them. (4.) Not the freemen only, but the hewers of wood and drawers of water, the meanest drudge they had among them. Note, As none are too great to come under the bonds of the covenant, so none are too mean to inherit the blessings of the covenant. In Christ no difference is made between <hi type="italic">bond and free,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.3.11">Col. iii. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">Art thou called being a servant? Care not for it,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.21">1 Cor. vii. 21</reference>. (5.) Not only those that were now present before God in this solemn assembly, but those also that were not here with them were taken into covenant (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">As with him that standeth here with us</hi> (so bishop Patrick thinks it should be rendered) <hi type="italic">so also with him, that is not here with us this day;</hi> that is, [1.] Those that tarried at home were included; though detained either by sickness or necessary business, they must not therefore think themselves disengaged; no, every Israelite shares in the common blessings. Those that tarry at home divide the spoil, and therefore every Israelite must own himself bound by the consent of the representative body. Those who cannot go up to the house of the Lord must keep up a spiritual communion with those that do, and be present in spirit when they are absent in body. [2.] The generations to come are included. Nay, one of the Chaldee paraphrasts reads it, <hi type="italic">All the generations that have been from the first days of the world, and all that shall arise to the end of the whole world, stand with us here this day.</hi> And so, taking this covenant as a typical dispensation of the covenant of grace, it is a noble testimony to the Mediator of that covenant, who is <hi type="italic">the same yesterday, to-day, and for ever.</hi> <div eID="gen3889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3890" type="x-p"/> II. The summary of this covenant. All the precepts and all the promises of the covenant are included in the covenant-relation between God and them, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.13">v. 13</reference>. That they should be appointed, raised up, <hi type="italic">established, for a people to him,</hi> to observe and obey him, to be devoted to him and dependent on him, and that he should be to them a God, according to the tenour of the covenant made with their fathers, to make them holy, high, and happy. Their fathers are here named, <hi type="italic">Abraham, Isaac,</hi> and <hi type="italic">Jacob,</hi> as examples of piety, which those were to set themselves to imitate who expected any benefit from the covenant made with them. Note, A due consideration of the relation we stand in to God as our God, and of the obligation we lie under as a people to him, is enough to bring us to all the duties and all the comforts of the covenant. <div eID="gen3890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3891" type="x-p"/> III. The principal design of the renewing of this covenant at this time was to fortify them against temptations to idolatry. Though other sins will be the sinner's ruin, yet this was the sin that was likely to be <hi type="italic">their</hi> ruin. Now concerning this he shows, <div eID="gen3891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3892" type="x-p"/> 1. The danger they were in of being tempted to it (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.16-Deut.29.17">v. 16, 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">You know we have dwelt in the land of Egypt,</hi> a country addicted to idolatry; and it were well if there were not among you some remains of the infection of that idolatry; we have <hi type="italic">passed by other nations, the Edomites, Moabites, &c.</hi> and have <hi type="italic">seen their abominations</hi> and <hi type="italic">their idols,</hi> and some among you, it may be, have liked them too well, and still hanker after them, and would rather worship a wooden god that they can see than an infinite Spirit whom they never saw." It is to be hoped that there were those among them who, the more they saw of these abominations and idols, the more they hated them; but there were those that were smitten with the sight of them, saw the accursed things and coveted them. <div eID="gen3892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3893" type="x-p"/> 2. The danger they were in if they yielded to the temptation. He gives them fair warning: it was at their peril if they forsook God to serve idols. If they would not be bound and held by the precepts of the covenant, they would find that the curses of the covenant would be strong enough to bind and hold them. <div eID="gen3893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3894" type="x-p"/> (1.) Idolatry would be the ruin of particular persons and their families, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.18-Deut.29.21">v. 18-21</reference>, where observe, <div eID="gen3894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3895" type="x-p"/> [1.] The sinner described, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.18">v. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He is one whose <hi type="italic">heart turns away from his God;</hi> there the mischief begins, in the <hi type="italic">evil heart of unbelief,</hi> which inclines men to <hi type="italic">depart from the living God</hi> to dead idols. Even to this sin men are tempted when they are drawn aside by their own lusts and fancies. Those that begin to turn from God, by neglecting their duty to him, are easily drawn to other gods: and those that serve other gods do certainly turn away from the true God; for he will admit of no rivals: he will be all or nothing. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He is <hi type="italic">a root that bears gall and wormwood;</hi> that is, he is a dangerous man, who, being himself poisoned with bad principles and inclinations, with a secret contempt of the God of Israel and his institutions and a veneration for the gods of the nations, endeavours, by all arts possible, to corrupt and poison others and draw them to idolatry: this is a man whose fruit is <hi type="italic">hemlock</hi> (so the word is translated, <reference osisRef="Hos.10.4">Hos. x. 4</reference>) and <hi type="italic">wormwood;</hi> it is very displeasing to God, and will be, to all that are seduced by him, <hi type="italic">bitterness in the latter end.</hi> This is referred to by the apostle, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.15">Heb. xii. 15</reference>, where he is in like manner cautioning us to take heed of those that would seduce us from the Christian faith; they are the weeds or tares in a field, which, if let alone, will overspread the whole field. A little of this leaven will be in danger of infecting the whole lump. <div eID="gen3895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3896" type="x-p"/> [2.] His security in the sun. He promises himself impunity, though he persists in his impiety, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.19">v. 19</reference>. Though he <hi type="italic">hears the words of the curse,</hi> so that he cannot plead ignorance of the danger, as other idolaters, yet even then he <hi type="italic">blesses himself in his own heart,</hi> thinks himself safe from the wrath of the God of Israel, under the protection of his idol-gods, and <hi type="italic">therefore says, "I shall have peace,</hi> though I be governed in my religion, not by God's institution, but by my own imagination, to add drunkenness to thirst, one act of wickedness to another." Idolaters were like drunkards, violently set upon their idols themselves and industrious to draw others in with them. Revellings commonly accompanied their idolatries (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.3">1 Pet. iv. 3</reference>), so that this speaks a woe to drunkards (especially the drunkards of Ephraim), who, when they are awake, being thirsty, <hi type="italic">seek it yet again,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.23.35">Prov. xxiii. 35</reference>. And those that made themselves drunk in honour of their idols were the worst of drunkards. Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> There are many who are under the curse of God and yet bless themselves; but it will soon be found that in blessing themselves they do but deceive themselves. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those are ripe for ruin, and there is little hope of their repentance, who have made themselves believe that they shall have peace though they go on in a sinful way. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> Drunkenness is a sin that hardens the heart, and debauches the conscience, as much as any other, a sin to which men are strangely tempted themselves even when they have lately felt the mischiefs of it, and to which they are strangely fond of drawing others, <reference osisRef="Hab.2.15">Hab. ii. 15</reference>. And such an ensnaring sin is idolatry. <div eID="gen3896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3897" type="x-p"/> [3.] God's just severity against him for the sin, and for the impious affront he put upon God in saying he should have peace though he went on, so giving the lie to eternal truth, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.4">Gen. iii. 4</reference>. There is scarcely a threatening in all the book of God that sounds more dreadful than this. O that presumptuous sinners would read it and tremble! For it is not a bug-bear to frighten children and fools, but a real declaration of the wrath of God against the ungodliness and the unrighteousness of men, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.20-Deut.29.21">v. 20, 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">First, The Lord shall not spare him.</hi> The days of his reprieve, which he abuses, will be shortened, and no mercy remembered in the midst of judgment. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The <hi type="italic">anger of the Lord, and his jealousy,</hi> which is the fiercest anger, <hi type="italic">shall smoke against him,</hi> like the smoke of a furnace. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The <hi type="italic">curses written</hi> shall <hi type="italic">lie upon him,</hi> not only light upon him to terrify him, but abide upon him, to sink him to the lowest hell, <reference osisRef="John.3.36">John iii. 36</reference>. <hi type="italic">Fourthly, His name shall be blotted out,</hi> that is, he himself shall be cut off, and his memory shall rot and perish with him. <hi type="italic">Fifthly,</hi> He shall be <hi type="italic">separated unto evil,</hi> which is the most proper notion of a curse; he shall be cut off from all happiness and all hope of it, and marked out for misery without remedy. And (<hi type="italic">lastly</hi>) All this <hi type="italic">according to the curses of the covenant,</hi> which are the most fearful curses, being the just revenges of abused grace. <div eID="gen3897" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3898" type="x-p"/> (2.) Idolatry would be the ruin of their nation; it would bring plagues upon the land that connived at this root of bitterness and received the infection; as far as the sin spread, the judgment should spread likewise. <div eID="gen3898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3899" type="x-p"/> [1.] The ruin is described. It begins with plagues and sicknesses (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.22">v. 22</reference>), to try if they will be reclaimed by less judgments; but, if not, it ends in a total overthrow, like that of Sodom, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.23">v. 23</reference>. As that valley, which had been like the garden of the Lord for fruitfulness, was turned into a lake of salt and sulphur, so should the land of Canaan be made desolate and barren, as it has been ever since the last destruction of it by the Romans. The lake of Sodom bordered closely upon the land of Israel, that by it they might be warned against the iniquity of Sodom; but, not taking the warning, they were made as like to Sodom in ruin as they had been in sin. <div eID="gen3899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3900" type="x-p"/> [2.] The reason of it is enquired into, and assigned. <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It would be enquired into by the <hi type="italic">generations to come</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.22">v. 22</reference>), who would find the state of their nation in all respects the reverse of what it had been, and, when they read both the history and the promise, would be astonished at the change. The stranger likewise, and the nations about them, as well as particular persons, would ask, <hi type="italic">Wherefore hath the Lord done thus unto this land?</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.29.24">v. 24</reference>. Great desolations are thus represented elsewhere as striking the spectators with amazement, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.8-1Kgs.9.9">1 Kings ix. 8, 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.22.8-Jer.22.9">Jer. xxii. 8, 9</reference>. It was time for the neighbours to tremble when judgment thus <hi type="italic">began at the house of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.17">1 Pet. iv. 17</reference>. The emphasis of the question is to be laid upon <hi type="italic">this land,</hi> the land of Canaan, this good land, the glory of all lands, this land flowing with milk and honey. A thousand pities that such a good land as this should be made desolate, but this is not all; it is this <hi type="italic">holy</hi> land, the land of Israel, a people in covenant with God; it is Immanuel's land, a land where God was known and worshipped, and yet thus wasted. Note, 1. It is no new thing for God to bring desolating judgments upon a people that in profession are near to him, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.2">Amos iii. 2</reference>. 2. He never does this without a good reason. 3. It concerns us to enquire into the reason, that we may give glory to God and take warning to ourselves. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The reason is here assigned, in answer to that enquiry. The matter would be so plain that all men would say, It was because they <hi type="italic">forsook the covenant of the Lord God of their fathers,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.29.25">v. 25</reference>. Note, God never forsakes any till they first forsake him. But those that desert the God of their fathers are justly cast out of the inheritance of their fathers. They went and <hi type="italic">served other gods</hi> (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.26">v. 26</reference>), gods that they had no acquaintance with, nor lay under any obligation to either in duty of gratitude; for God has not given the creatures to be served by us, but to serve us; nor have they done any good to us (as some read it), more than what God has enabled them to do; to the Creator therefore we are debtors, and not to the creatures. It was for this that God was angry with them (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.27">v. 27</reference>), and <hi type="italic">rooted them out in anger,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.29.28">v. 28</reference>. So that, how dreadful soever the desolation was, the Lord was righteous in it, which is acknowledged, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.11-Dan.9.14">Dan. ix. 11-14</reference>. "Thus" (says Mr. Ainsworth) "the law of Moses leaves sinners under the curse, and <hi type="italic">rooted out of the Lord's land;</hi> but the grace of Christ towards penitent believing sinners plants them again <hi type="italic">upon their land, and they shall no more be pulled up,</hi> being kept by the power of God," <reference osisRef="Amos.9.15">Amos ix. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen3900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen3901" type="x-p"/> [3.] He concludes his prophecy of the Jews' rejection just as St. Paul concludes his discourse on the same subject, when it began to be fulfilled (<reference osisRef="Rom.11.33">Rom. xi. 33</reference>), <hi type="italic">How unsearchable are God's judgments, and his ways past finding out!</hi> So here (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.29">v. 29</reference>), <hi type="italic">Secret things belong to the Lord our God.</hi> Some make it to be one sentence, <hi type="italic">The secret things of the Lord our God are revealed to us and to our children,</hi> as far as we are concerned to know them, and <hi type="italic">he hath not dealt so with other nations:</hi> but we make it two sentences, by which, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> We are forbidden curiously to enquire into the secret counsels of God and to determine concerning them. A full answer is given to that question, <hi type="italic">Wherefore has the Lord done thus to this land?</hi> sufficient to justify God and admonish us. But if any ask further why God would be at such a vast expense of miracles to form such a people, whose apostasy and ruin he plainly foresaw, why he did not by his almighty grace prevent it, or what he intends yet to do with them, let such know that these are questions which cannot be answered, and therefore are not fit to be asked. It is presumption in us to pry into the <hi type="italic">Arcana imperii—the mysteries of government,</hi> and to enquire into the reasons of state which <hi type="italic">it is not for us to know.</hi> See <reference osisRef="Acts.1.7">Acts i. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.21.22">John xxi. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.18">Col. ii. 18</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> We are directed and encouraged diligently to enquire into that which God has made known: things <hi type="italic">revealed belong to us and to our children.</hi> Note, 1. Though God has kept much of his counsel secret, yet there is enough revealed to satisfy and save us. He has <hi type="italic">kept back nothing that is profitable for us,</hi> but that only which it is good for us to be ignorant of. 2. We ought to acquaint ourselves, and our children, too, with the things of God that are revealed. We are not only allowed to search into them, but are concerned to do so. They are things which we and ours are nearly interested in. They are the rules we are to live by, the grants we are to live upon; and therefore we are to learn them diligently ourselves, and to teach them diligently to our children. 3. All our knowledge must be in order to practice, for this is the end of all divine revelation, not to furnish us with curious subjects of speculation and discourse, with which to entertain ourselves and our friends, <hi type="italic">but that we may do all the words of this law,</hi> and be blessed in our deed.  <chapter eID="Deut.29"/> <div eID="gen3901" type="x-p"/>

entries.61454ebcee464a3059601cc8472aacd0d33897d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1908"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 29</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Deut.29.1-Deut.29.29">De 29:1-29</reference>. An Exhortation to Obedience.</title> <div sID="gen2534" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1908"/><hi type="bold">1. These are the words of the covenant--</hi>The discourse of Moses is continued, and the subject of that discourse was Israel's covenant with God, the privileges it conferred, and the obligations it imposed.<div eID="gen2534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2535" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">beside the covenant which he made with them in Horeb--</hi>It was substantially the same; but it was renewed now, in different circumstances. They had violated its conditions. Moses rehearses these, that they might have a better knowledge of its conditions and be more disposed to comply with them. <div eID="gen2535" type="x-p"/>
entries.aa1e3809d82b9ac171bfb296f5d753e10bd57809: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1909"/><div sID="gen2536" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1909"/><hi type="bold">2. Moses called unto all Israel, ... Ye have seen all that the Lord did, &c.--</hi>This appeal to the experience of the people, though made generally, was applicable only to that portion of them who had been very young at the period of the Exodus, and who remembered the marvellous transactions that preceded and followed that era. Yet, alas! <hi type="bold">those wonderful events made no good impression upon them (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.4">De 29:4</reference>). They were strangers to that grace of wisdom which is liberally given to all who ask it; and their insensibility was all the more inexcusable that so many miracles had been performed which might have led to a certain conviction of the presence and the power of God with them. The preservation of their clothes and shoes, the supply of daily food and fresh water--</hi>these continued without interruption or diminution during so many years' sojourn in the desert. They were miracles which unmistakably proclaimed the immediate hand of God and were performed for the express purpose of training them to a practical knowledge of, and habitual confidence in, Him. Their experience of this extraordinary goodness and care, together with their remembrance of the brilliant successes by which, with little exertion or loss on their part, God enabled them to acquire the valuable territory on which they stood, is mentioned again to enforce a faithful adherence to the covenant, as the direct and sure means of obtaining its promised blessings. <div eID="gen2536" type="x-p"/>
entries.10b519d6fe48c784e1556343eec797fd8debbc6b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv1910"/><div sID="gen2537" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv1910"/><hi type="bold">10-29. Ye stand this day all of you before the Lord your God--</hi>The whole congregation of Israel, of all ages and conditions, all--young as well as old; menials as well as masters; native Israelites as well as naturalized strangers--all were assembled before the tabernacle to renew the Sinaitic covenant. None of them were allowed to consider themselves as exempt from the terms of that national compact, lest any lapsing into idolatry might prove a root of bitterness, spreading its noxious seed and corrupt influence all around (compare <reference osisRef="Heb.12.15">He 12:15</reference>). It was of the greatest consequence thus to reach the heart and conscience of everyone, for some might delude themselves with the vain idea that by taking the oath (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.12">De 29:12</reference>) by which they engaged themselves in covenant with God, they would surely secure its blessings. Then, even though they would not rigidly adhere to His worship and commands, but would follow the devices and inclinations of their own hearts, yet they would think that He would wink at such liberties and not punish them. It was of the greatest consequence to impress all with the strong and abiding conviction, that while the covenant of grace had special blessings belonging to it, it at the same time had curses in reserve for transgressors, the infliction of which would be as certain, as lasting and severe. This was the advantage contemplated in the law being rehearsed a second time. The picture of a once rich and flourishing region, blasted and doomed in consequence of the sins of its inhabitants, is very striking, and calculated to awaken awe in every reflecting mind. Such is, and long has been, the desolate state of Palestine; and, in looking at its ruined cities, its blasted coast, its naked mountains, its sterile and parched soil--all the sad and unmistakable evidences of a land lying under a curse--numbers of travellers from Europe, America, and the Indies ("strangers from a far country," <reference osisRef="Deut.29.22">De 29:22</reference>) in the present day see that the Lord has executed His threatening. Who can resist the conclusion that it has been inflicted "because the inhabitants had forsaken the covenant of the Lord God of their fathers. ... and the anger of the Lord was kindled against this land, to bring upon it all the curses that are written in this book"? <div eID="gen2537" type="x-p"/>

entries.e05e2360b7daf18900d88de6b0426a2807af3b95: <div eID="gen7067" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen7068" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7069" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7069" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7068" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7070" type="x-p"/> A recapitulation of God's gracious dealings with Israel, <reference osisRef="Deu.29.1-Deu.29.8">Deu 29:1-8</reference>. An exhortation to obedience, and to enter into covenant with their God, that they and their posterity may be established in the good land, <reference osisRef="Deu.29.9-Deu.29.15">Deu 29:9-15</reference>. They are to remember the abominations of Egypt, and to avoid them, <reference osisRef="Deu.29.16">Deu 29:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.29.17">Deu 29:17</reference>. He who hardens his heart, when he hears these curses, shall be utterly consumed, <reference osisRef="Deu.29.18-Deu.29.21">Deu 29:18-21</reference>. Their posterity shall be astonished at the desolations that shall fall upon them, <reference osisRef="Deu.29.22">Deu 29:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deu.29.23">Deu 29:23</reference>; shall inquire the reason, and shall be informed that the Lord has done thus to them because of their disobedience and idolatry, <reference osisRef="Deu.29.24-Deu.29.28">Deu 29:24-28</reference>. A caution against prying too curiously into the secrets of the Divine providence, and to be contented with what God has revealed, <reference osisRef="Deu.29.29">Deu 29:29</reference>. <div eID="gen7070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7071" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen7071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7072" type="x-p"/> These are the words of the covenant - This verse seems properly to belong to the preceding chapter, as a widely different subject is taken up at <reference osisRef="Deu.29.2">Deu 29:2</reference> of this; and it is distinguished as the 69th verse in some of the most correct copies of the Hebrew Bible. <div eID="gen7072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7073" type="x-p"/> Commanded Moses to make - לכרת lichroth, to cut, alluding to the covenant sacrifice which was offered on the occasion and divided, as is explained, <reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">Gen 15:18</reference> (note). <div eID="gen7073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7074" type="x-p"/> Beside the covenant which he made - in Horeb - What is mentioned here is an additional institution to the ten words given on Horeb; and the curses denounced here are different from those denounced against the transgressors of the decalogue.
entries.45fe74fcdeb51ea8d4d7ce8de30f86c91b64669d: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen7074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7075" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath not given you a heart, etc. - Some critics read this verse interrogatively: And hath not God given you a heart, etc.? because they suppose that God could not reprehend them for the non-performance of a duty, when he had neither given them a mind to perceive the obligation of it, nor strength to perform it, had that obligation been known. Though this is strictly just, yet there is no need for the interrogation, as the words only imply that they had not such a heart, etc., not because God had not given them all the means of knowledge, and helps of his grace and Spirit, which were necessary; but they had not made a faithful use of their advantages, and therefore they had not that wise, loving, and obedient heart which they otherwise might have had. If they had had such a heart, it would have been God's gift, for he is the author of all good; and that they had not such a heart was a proof that they had grieved his Spirit, and abused the grace which he had afforded them to produce that gracious change, the want of which is here deplored. Hence God himself is represented as grieved because they were unchanged and disobedient: "O that there were such a heart in them, that they would fear me, and keep all my commandments always, that it might be well with them and with their children for ever!" See <reference osisRef="Deu.5.29">Deu 5:29</reference> (note), and the note there.
entries.aa07ba1fc7d91e7f5d16f8a0358f5dda2f6e8837: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen7075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7076" type="x-p"/> Your clothes are not waxen old - See on <reference osisRef="Deu.8.4">Deu 8:4</reference> (note).
entries.a9b110c9e3c440c4a7c9e621aa8ec3b61ce790c4: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen7076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7077" type="x-p"/> Ye have not eaten bread, etc. - That is, ye have not been supported in an ordinary providential way; I have been continually working miracles for you, that ye might know that I am the Lord. Thus we find that God had furnished them with all the means of this knowledge, and that the means were ineffectual, not because they were not properly calculated to answer God's gracious purpose, but because the people were not workers with God; consequently they received the grace of God in vain. See <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.1">2Cor 6:1</reference>.
entries.413ab1180df7c11b533f9b2917330a4b596b439c: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen7077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7078" type="x-p"/> Ye stand - all of you before the Lord - They were about to enter into a covenant with God; and as a covenant implies two parties contracting, God is represented as being present, and they and all their families, old and young, come before him.
entries.846e6c124c00cfacd25972e48f2ce5146adc6576: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen7078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7079" type="x-p"/> That thou shouldest enter - לעבר leaber, to pass through, that is, between the separated parts of the covenant sacrifice. See <reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">Gen 15:18</reference> (note). <div eID="gen7079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7080" type="x-p"/> And into his oath - Thus we find that in a covenant were these seven particulars: <div eID="gen7080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7081" type="x-p"/> 1. The parties about to contract were considered as being hitherto separated. <div eID="gen7081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7082" type="x-p"/> 2. They now agree to enter into a state of close and permanent amity. <div eID="gen7082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7083" type="x-p"/> 3. They meet together in a solemn manner for this purpose. <div eID="gen7083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7084" type="x-p"/> 4. A sacrifice is offered to God on the occasion, for the whole is a religious act. <div eID="gen7084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7085" type="x-p"/> 5. The victim is separated exactly into two equal parts, the separation being in the direction of the spine; and those parts are laid opposite to each other, sufficient room being allowed for the contracting parties to pass between them. <div eID="gen7085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7086" type="x-p"/> 6. The contracting parties meet in the victim, and the conditions of the covenant by which they are to be mutually bound are recited. <div eID="gen7086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7087" type="x-p"/> 7. An oath is taken by these parties that they shall punctually and faithfully perform their respective conditions, and thus the covenant is made and ratified. See <reference osisRef="Jer.34.18">Jer 34:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.34.19">Jer 34:19</reference>, and the notes on <reference osisRef="Gen.6.18">Gen 6:18</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Gen.15.18">Gen 15:18</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Exo.29.45">Exo 29:45</reference> (note); Leviticus 26 (note).
entries.8949fe0aa2506e63ab6dee3bf7753fc08d20076a: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen7087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7088" type="x-p"/> Him that standeth here - The present generation. Him that is not here - all future generations of this people.
entries.c405398b4e50a77b79713e5296b54138e91dd289: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen7088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7089" type="x-p"/> A root that beareth gall and wormwood - That is, as the apostle expresses it, <reference osisRef="Heb.3.12">Heb 3:12</reference>, An evil heart of unbelief departing from the living God; for to this place he evidently refers. It may also signify false doctrines, or idolatrous persons among themselves.
entries.a88c022c6cddf5a513d12ae0bc0363ed3d322f03: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen7089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7090" type="x-p"/> To add drunkenness to thirst - A proverbial expression denoting the utmost indulgence in all sensual gratifications.
entries.5259521cd1191d5f94171c475735ac5d60a2f791: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen7090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7091" type="x-p"/> Gods - whom he had not given unto them - This is an unhappy translation. Houbigant renders the original words ולו חלק להם velo chalak lahem, et quibuscum nulla eis societas, "And with whom they had no society;" and falls unmercifully on Le Clerc because he had translated it, From whom they had received no benefits. I must differ from both these great men, because I think they differ from the text. חלק chalak signifies a portion, lot, inheritance, and God is frequently represented in Scripture as the portion or inheritance of his people. Here, therefore, I think the original should be rendered, And there was no portion to them, that is, the gods they served could neither supply their wants nor save their souls - they were no portion.
entries.cbdcebb587d0cb89da03f592232c11aa4aeb22e1: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen7091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7092" type="x-p"/> The secret things belong unto the Lord, etc. - This verse has been variously translated. Houbigant renders it thus: Quae apud Dominum nostrum abscondita sunt, nobis ea filiisque nostris palam facta sunt ad multas aetates, "The things which were hidden with the Lord our God, are made manifest to us and our children for many generations." I am not satisfied with this interpretation, and find that the passage was not so understood by any of the ancient versions. The simple general meaning seems to be this: "What God has thought proper to reveal, he has revealed; what he has revealed is essential to the well-being of man, and this revelation is intended not for the present time merely, nor for one people, but for all succeeding generations. The things which he has not revealed concern not man but God alone, and are therefore not to be inquired after." Thus, then, the things that are hidden belong unto the Lord, those that are revealed belong unto us and our children. But possibly the words here refer to the subjects of these chapters, as if he had said, "Apostasy from God and his truth is possible. When a national apostasy among us may take place, is known only to God; but he has revealed himself to us and our children that we may do all the words of this law, and so prevent the dreadful evils that shall fall on the disobedient." <div eID="gen7092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7093" type="x-p"/> The Jews have always considered these verses as containing subjects of the highest importance to them, and have affixed marks to the original לנו ולבנינו lanu ulebaneynu, "to Us and to our Children," in order to fix the attention of the reader on truths which affect them individually, and not them only, but the whole of their posterity.  <chapter eID="Deut.29"/> <div eID="gen7093" type="x-p"/>

entries.e5d656934f28cf2625339d6d3e016efb5ffc816f: <div eID="gen2518" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Conclusion of the Covenant in the Land of Moab - Deuteronomy 29-30</title> <div sID="gen2519" type="x-p"/> The addresses which follow in ch. 29 and 30 are announced in the heading in <reference osisRef="Deut.29.1">Deu 29:1</reference> as “<hi type="italic">words</hi> (addresses) <hi type="italic">of the covenant which Jehovah commanded Moses to make with the children of Israel, beside the covenant which He made with them in Horeb,</hi>” and consist, according to Deu 29:10., in a solemn appeal to all the people to enter into the covenant which the Lord made with them that day; that is to say, it consisted literally in a renewed declaration of the covenant which the Lord had concluded with the nation at Horeb, or in a fresh obligation imposed upon the nation to keep the covenant which had been concluded at Horeb, by the offering of sacrifices and the sprinkling of the people with the sacrificial blood (Ex 24). There was no necessity for any repetition of this act, because, notwithstanding the frequent transgressions on the part of the nation, it had not been abrogated on the part of God, but still remained in full validity and force. The obligation binding upon the people to fulfil the covenant is introduced by Moses with an appeal to all that the Lord had done for Israel (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.2-Deut.29.9">Deu 29:2-9</reference>); and this is followed by a summons to enter into the covenant which the Lord was concluding with the now, that He might be their God, and fulfil His promises concerning them (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.10-Deut.29.15">Deu 29:10-15</reference>), with a repeated allusion to the punishment which threatened them in case of apostasy (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.16-Deut.29.29">Deu 29:16-29</reference>), and the eventual restoration on the ground of sincere repentance and return to the Lord (<reference osisRef="Deut.30.1-Deut.30.14">Deu 30:1-14</reference>), and finally another solemn adjuration, with a blessing and a curse before them, to make choice of the blessing (<reference osisRef="Deut.30.15-Deut.30.20">Deu 30:15-20</reference>). <div eID="gen2519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2520" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Deut.29.2-Deut.29.4">Deu  29:2-4</reference> <div eID="gen2520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2521" type="x-p"/> The introduction in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Deut.29.2">Deu 29:2</reference></hi> resembles that in Deu 5:1. “<hi type="italic">All Israel</hi>” is the nation in all its members (see <reference osisRef="Deut.29.10">Deu 29:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.11">Deu 29:11</reference>). - Israel had no doubt seen the mighty acts of the Lord in Egypt (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Deut.29.2">Deu 29:2</reference></hi> and <reference osisRef="Deut.29.3">Deu 29:3</reference>; cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.4.34">Deu 4:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.7.19">Deu 7:19</reference>), but Jehovah had not given them a heart, i.e., understanding, to perceive, eyes to see, and ears to hear, until this day. With this complaint, Moses does not intend to excuse the previous want of susceptibility on the part of the nation to the manifestations of grace on the part of the Lord, but simply to explain the necessity for the repeated allusion to the gracious acts of God, and to urge the people to lay them truly to heart. “By reproving the dulness of the past, he would stimulate them to a desire to understand: just as if he had said, that for a long time they had been insensible to so many miracles, and therefore they ought not to delay any longer, but to arouse themselves to hearken better unto God” (<hi type="italic">Calvin</hi>). The Lord had not yet given the people an understanding heart, because the people had not yet asked for it, simply because the need of it was not felt (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.4.26">Deu 4:26</reference>).
entries.199041d0bb7ac1a94f97f7807abba4bc406098cf: <reference osisRef="Deut.29.5-Deut.29.8">Deu 29:5-8</reference> <div eID="gen2521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2522" type="x-p"/> With the appeal to the gracious guidance of Israel by God through the desert, the address of Moses passes imperceptibly into an address from the Lord, just as in Deu 11:14. (On <reference osisRef="Deut.29.5">Deu 29:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.6">Deu 29:6</reference>, vid., <reference osisRef="Deut.8.3-Deut.8.4">Deu 8:3-4</reference>; on <reference osisRef="Deut.29.7">Deu 29:7</reference>, vid., Deu 2:26., and Deu 3:1. and Deu 3:12.).
entries.19480965b7325bbf727a463125343bab428501ac: <reference osisRef="Deut.29.9">Deu 29:9</reference> <div eID="gen2522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2523" type="x-p"/> These benefits from the Lord demanded obedience and fidelity. “<hi type="italic">Keep the words of this covenant</hi>,” etc. (cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.8.18">Deu 8:18</reference>). השׂכּיל, to act wisely (as in <reference osisRef="Deut.32.29">Deu 32:29</reference>), bearing in mind, however, that Jehovah Himself is the wisdom of Israel (<reference osisRef="Deut.4.6">Deu 4:6</reference>), and the search for this wisdom brings prosperity and salvation (cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.1.7-Josh.1.8">Jos 1:7-8</reference>). <div eID="gen2523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2524" type="x-p"/> Summons to enter into the covenant of the Lord, namely, to enter inwardly, to make the covenant an affair of the heart and life.
entries.5946b48d793fe789d8bc5f33e989361df9b53a42: <reference osisRef="Deut.29.10">Deu 29:10</reference> <div eID="gen2524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2525" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">To-day</hi>,” when the covenant-law and covenant-right were laid before them, the whole nation stood before the Lord without a single exception - the heads and the tribes, the elders and the officers, all the men of Israel. The two members are parallel. The heads of the people are the elders and officers, and the tribes consist of all the men. The rendering given by the lxx and Syriac (also in the English version: Tr.), “<hi type="italic">heads</hi> (captains) <hi type="italic">of your tribes</hi>,” is at variance with the language.
entries.4b6447fcbae960dbdb078c9d29874a0f9e46ac51: <reference osisRef="Deut.29.11">Deu 29:11</reference> <div eID="gen2525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2526" type="x-p"/> The covenant of the Lord embraced, however, not only the men of Israel, but also the wives and children, and the stranger who had attached himself to Israel, such as the Egyptians who came out with Israel (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.38">Exo 12:38</reference>; Num 11:4), and the Midianites who joined the Israelites with Hobab (Num 10:29), down to the very lowest servant, “<hi type="italic">from thy hewer of wood to thy drawer of water</hi>” (cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.9.21">Jos 9:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.9.27">Jos 9:27</reference>).
entries.c8488e49f426565bdd9b587091519688e358fb55: <reference osisRef="Deut.29.12">Deu 29:12</reference> <div eID="gen2526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2527" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">That thou shouldest enter into the covenant of the Lord thy God, and the engagement on oath, which the Lord thy God concludeth with thee to-day</hi>.” עבר with בּ, as in <reference osisRef="Job.33.28">Job 33:28</reference>, “to enter into,” expresses entire entrance, which goes completely through the territory entered, and is more emphatic than בברית בּוא   (<reference osisRef="2Chr.15.12">2Ch 15:12</reference>). “Into the oath:” the covenant confirmed with an oath, covenants being always accompanied with oaths (vid., <reference osisRef="Gen.26.28">Gen 26:28</reference>).
entries.8edca95de1f1e3217373af55ab44be26be8a661b: <reference osisRef="Deut.29.13">Deu 29:13</reference> <div eID="gen2527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2528" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">That He may set thee up</hi> (exalt thee) <hi type="italic">to-day into a people for Himself, and that He may be</hi> (become) <hi type="italic">unto thee a God</hi>” (vid., <reference osisRef="Deut.28.9">Deu 28:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.27.9">Deu 27:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.19.5-Exod.19.6">Exo 19:5-6</reference>).
entries.c1f15b3dce8c272bf2032fa8fa9833dd32f64c96: <reference osisRef="Deut.29.14-Deut.29.15">Deu 29:14-15</reference> <div eID="gen2528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2529" type="x-p"/> This covenant Moses made not only with those who are present, but with all whether present or not; for it was to embrace not only those who were living then, but their descendants also, to become a covenant of blessing for all nations (cf. <reference osisRef="Acts.2.39">Act 2:39</reference>, and the intercession of Christ in Joh 17:20).
entries.9a15ffdcfe7f5401a1d5185e10982dcbfc474d6e: <reference osisRef="Deut.29.16-Deut.29.17">Deu 29:16-17</reference> <div eID="gen2529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2530" type="x-p"/> The summons to enter into the covenant of the Lord is explained by Moses first of all by an exposition of the evil results which would follow from apostasy from the Lord, or the breach of His covenant. This exposition he introduces with an allusion to the experience of the people with reference to the worthlessness of idols, both in Egypt itself, and upon their march through the nations, whose territory they passed through (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.16">Deu 29:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.29.17">Deu 29:17</reference>). The words, “<hi type="italic">for ye have learned how we dwelt in Egypt, and passed through the nations...and have seen their abominations and their idols</hi>” (<hi type="italic">gillulim</hi>: lit., clods, see <reference osisRef="Lev.26.30">Lev 26:30</reference>), have this signification: In our abode in Egypt, and upon our march through different lands, ye have become acquainted with the idols of these nations, that they are not gods, but only wood and stone (see at <reference osisRef="Deut.4.28">Deu 4:28</reference>), silver and gold. את־אשׁר, as in <reference osisRef="Deut.9.7">Deu 9:7</reference>, literally “ye know that which we dwelt,' i.e., know what our dwelling there showed, what experience we gained there of the nature of heathen idols.
entries.28e1c302430b9a444d8fea910f9ebe0ad606df14: <reference osisRef="Deut.29.18-Deut.29.19">Deu 29:18-19</reference> <div eID="gen2530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2531" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">That there may not be among you</hi>,” etc.: this sentence may be easily explained by introducing a thought which may be easily supplied, such as “consider this,” or “do not forget what ye have seen, that no one, either man or woman, family or tribe, may turn away from Jehovah our God.” - “<hi type="italic">That there may not be a root among you which bears poison and wormwood as fruit</hi>.” A striking image of the destructive fruit borne by idolatry (cf. <reference osisRef="Heb.12.15">Heb 12:15</reference>). Rosh stands for a plant of a very bitter taste, as we may see from the frequency with which it is combined with לענה, wormwood: it is not, strictly speaking, a poisonous plant, although the word is used in <reference osisRef="Job.20.16">Job 20:16</reference> to denote the poison of serpents, because, in the estimation of a Hebrew, bitterness and poison were kindred terms. There is no other passage in which it can be shown to have the meaning “poison.” The sense of the figure is given in plain terms in <reference osisRef="Deut.29.19">Deu 29:19</reference>, “<hi type="italic">that no one when he hears the words of this oath may bless himself in his heart, saying, I will prosper with me, for I walk in the firmness of my heart</hi>.” To bless himself in his heart is to congratulate himself. שׁרירוּת, firmness, a <hi type="italic">vox media</hi>; in Syriac, firmness, in a good sense, equivalent to truth; in Hebrew, generally in a bad sense, denoting hardness of heart; and this is the sense in which Moses uses it here. - “<hi type="italic">To sweep away that which is saturated with the thirsty:</hi>” a proverbial expression, of which very different interpretations have been given (see <hi type="italic">Rosenmüller ad h.</hi> <hi type="italic">l.</hi>), taken no doubt from the land and transferred to persons or souls; so that we might supply <hi type="italic">Nephesh</hi> in this sense, “to destroy all, both those who have drunk its poison, and those also who are still thirsting for it” (<hi type="italic">Knobel</hi>). But even if we were to supply ארץ (the land), we should not have to think of the land itself, but simply of its inhabitants, so that the thought would still remain the same.
entries.17d91f62d6e56dc0fe6453a0acdef47fd8e9b6a9: <reference osisRef="Deut.29.20-Deut.29.21">Deu 29:20-21</reference> “For the Lord will not forgive him (who thinks or speaks in this way); <hi type="italic">but then will His anger smoke </hi>(break forth in fire; vid., (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.1">Psa 74:1</reference>), <hi type="italic">and His jealousy against that man, and the whole curse of the law will lie upon him, that his name may be blotted out under heaven</hi> (vid., <reference osisRef="Deut.25.19">Deu 25:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.17.14">Exo 17:14</reference>). “<hi type="italic">The Lord will separate him unto evil from all the tribes</hi>, - so that he will be shut out from the covenant nation, and from its salvation, and be exposed to destruction - <hi type="italic">according to all the curses of the covenant</hi>.” Although the pronominal suffix refers primarily to the man, it also applies, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.29.18">Deu 29:18</reference>, to the woman, the family, and the tribe. “That is written,” etc., as in <reference osisRef="Deut.28.58">Deu 28:58</reference>, Deu 28:61.
entries.3823e79672c45448d1a80631ec680807cfe8d7ae: <reference osisRef="Deut.29.22-Deut.29.23">Deu 29:22-23</reference> <div eID="gen2531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2532" type="x-p"/> How thoroughly Moses was filled with the thought, that not only individuals, but whole families, and in fact the greater portion of the nation, would fall into idolatry, is evident from the further expansion of the threat which follows, and in which he foresees in the Spirit, and foretells, the extermination of whole families, and the devastation of the land by distant nations; as in <reference osisRef="Lev.26.31">Lev 26:31</reference>-32. Future generations of Israel, and the stranger from a distant land, when they saw the strokes of the Lord which burst upon the land, and the utter desolation of the land, would ask whence this devastation, and receive the reply, The Lord had smitten the land thus in His anger, because its inhabitants (the Israelites) had forsaken His covenant. With regard to the construction, observe that ואמר, in <reference osisRef="Deut.29.22">Deu 29:22</reference>, is resumed in ואמרוּ, in <reference osisRef="Deut.29.24">Deu 29:24</reference>, the subject of <reference osisRef="Deut.29.22">Deu 29:22</reference> being expanded into the general notion, “all nations” (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.24">Deu 29:24</reference>). With וראוּ, in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Deut.29.22">Deu 29:22</reference></hi>, a parenthetical clause is inserted, giving the reason for the main thought, in the form of a circumstantial clause; and to this there is attached, by a loose apposition in <reference osisRef="Deut.29.23">Deu 29:23</reference>, a still further picture of the divine strokes according to their effect upon the land. The nouns in <reference osisRef="Deut.29.23">Deu 29:23</reference>, “<hi type="italic">brimstone and salt burning</hi>,” are in apposition to the strokes (plagues), and so far depend upon “they see.” The description is borrowed from the character of the Dead Sea and its vicinity, to which there is an express allusion in the words, “<hi type="italic">like the overthrow of Sodom</hi>,” etc., i.e., of the towns of the vale of Siddim (see at <reference osisRef="Gen.14.2">Gen 14:2</reference>), which resembled paradise, the garden of Jehovah, before their destruction (vid., <reference osisRef="Gen.13.10">Gen 13:10</reference> and Gen 19:24.).
entries.b505164309c19cf0129be59e2d016eb65f289541: <reference osisRef="Deut.29.24-Deut.29.25">Deu 29:24-25</reference> <div eID="gen2532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2533" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">What is this great burning of wrath?</hi>” i.e., what does it mean - whence does it come? The reply to such a question would be (<reference osisRef="Deut.29.25-Deut.29.29">Deu 29:25-29</reference>): The inhabitants of the land have forsaken the covenant of the Lord, the God of their fathers; therefore has the wrath of the Lord burned over the land.
entries.c95f48fc6c58a2de266d71f4117f5de5a6b6f23c: <reference osisRef="Deut.29.26-Deut.29.29">Deu 29:26-29</reference> <div eID="gen2533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen2534" type="x-p"/> “<hi type="italic">Gods which God had not assigned them</hi>” (vid., <reference osisRef="Deut.4.19">Deu 4:19</reference>). “All the curses,” etc., are the curses contained in <reference osisRef="Deut.28.15-Deut.28.68">Deut 28:15-68</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.26.14">Lev 26:14</reference>-38. - Those who give the answer close their address in <reference osisRef="Deut.29.29">Deu 29:29</reference> with an expression of pious submission and solemn admonition. “<hi type="italic">That which is hidden belongs to the Lord our God</hi> (is His affair), <hi type="italic">and that which is revealed belongs to us and our children for ever, to do</hi> (that we may do) <hi type="italic">all the words of this law</hi>.” That which is revealed includes the law with its promises and threats; consequently that which is hidden can only refer to the mode in which God will carry out in the future His counsel and will, which He has revealed in the law, and complete His work of salvation notwithstanding the apostasy of the people.<note placement="foot">What the <hi type="italic">puncta extraordinaria</hi> above (ע)ד וּלבנינוּ לנוּ mean, is uncertain. <hi type="italic">Hiller's</hi> conjecture is the most probable, “that they are intended to indicate a various reading, formed by the omission of eleven consonants, and the transposition of the rest עולם והנגדלות (<hi type="italic">at magnalia saeculi sunt</hi>);” whereas there is no foundation for <hi type="italic">Lightfoot's</hi> notion, that “they served as a warning, that we should not wish to pry with curiosity into the secret things of God, but should be content with His revealed will,” - a notion which rests upon the supposition that the points are inspired.</note>  <chapter eID="Deut.29"/> <div eID="gen2534" type="x-p"/>

entries.19bf432453656f0dee9debda6ab96f59c072713c: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.29.2" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.29.2" sID="gen8783" type="section"/> <div sID="gen8784" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">2.</hi> <hi type="italic">And Moses called unto all Israel.</hi> This passage also may be fitly referred to the preface of the Law, since its tendency is to recommend it, and to instruct and prepare the people’s minds to be teachable. It takes its commencement from the divine blessings, which they had experienced as well in their exodus as in their forty years’ wanderings; for it would have been the height of baseness and ingratitude not to devote themselves to a Deliverer who had dealt so graciously with them. And surely it was an inestimable sign of His paternal love towards them, that He should have arrayed Himself against so very powerful a king for His servants’ sake. Finally, lest there should be any question as to their deliverance<hi type="italic">, </hi>he enlarges upon the power which God displayed therein, in magnificent terms of praise according with its dignity.<div eID="gen8784" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.29.2" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen8783" osisID="Deut.29.2" type="section"/>
entries.5d148139872df4b7768aed510ecb6c9414fe610b:
4. Yet the Lord hath not given. By reproaching them with their past stupidity, he stirs up their desire for a better understanding, as if he had said, that they had been too long indifferent to so many miracles, and therefore they should no longer delay to rouse themselves, etc., to give greater heed to God; not because they had been so senseless that His acts had altogether escaped their notice, but because all acknowledgment of them had immediately come to an end. For, just as the drunken man, or one suffering from lethargy, when he hears a cry, raises his head for a moment, and opens his eyes, and then relapses into a state of torpor, so the people had never seriously applied their minds to consider God’s works; and when they had been aroused by some miracle, had immediately sunk back into forgetfulness, wherefore there is good cause why Moses should seek to awaken them from their dulness and stupidity by various methods. But he does not merely condemn their senselessness, and blindness, and deafness, but declares that they were thus senseless, and blind, and deaf, because they were not inspired with grace from above to profit duly by so many lessons. Thence we learn that a clear and powerful understanding is a special gift of the Spirit, since men are ever blind even in the brightest light, until they have been enlightened by God. What Moses relates of the Israelites, is unquestionably common to us all. He declares, then, that they were not induced by the conspicuous glory of God to fear and worship Him, because He had not given them either mind, or eyes, or ears. It is true that at man’s creation He had naturally bestowed upon him a mind, and ears, and eyes; but Moses means, that whatever innate light we have, is either hidden or lost, so that, as far as regards the highest point of wisdom, all our senses lie useless. True that in nature’s corruption, the light still shineth in darkness, but it is light which is soon obscured; therefore, the entire understanding and faculty of reason, in which men glory and pique themselves, is nought but smoke and darkness. Well then may David ask that his eyes may be opened to behold the secrets of the Law.
The references here are to Psalm 19:13, and 18:24, (in the Fr. 14.) There may be allusion to 19:12, and 18:28. See Calvin’s comments on these passages.
(Psalm 119:18.) Still this defect by no means frees us from blame; because (as we are told) none have wisdom, but those to whom it is given by the Father of lights; for we are ignorant
“Desipimus.” — Lat. “Ainsi hebetez, et desprouvez de sens.” — Fr.
through our own fault. Besides, every one is sufficiently, and more than sufficiently convicted by his own conscience, that his ignorance is closely connected with pride and indolence, and is therefore voluntary. The word heart is not here used for the seat of the affections, but for the mind itself, which is the intellectual faculty of the soul.
entries.5276a1d905ee4d6234955160f266fe0bf3eed63a: <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.29.5" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Deut.29.5" sID="gen8789" type="section"/> <div sID="gen8790" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">5.</hi> <hi type="italic">And I have led you.</hi> He descends to the blessings with which He had continually visited His people during the course of forty years. Yet he does not recount them all, but contents himself with a few of the most remarkable instances, viz., that their clothes had not been worn out by age, and that they had been fed from heaven, when no sustenance was to be obtained from the fruits of the earth. He reminds them that God’s glory had been manifested by these testimonies, in order that they might submit themselves to His rule.<div eID="gen8790" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Deut.29.5" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen8789" osisID="Deut.29.5" type="section"/>
entries.a7456d0fdaec91bc6524875d60bdfd717a5c36c0:
7. And when ye came unto this place. This, a third instance (of God’s goodness), because He had smitten the first enemies, who encountered them to impede their passage, and thus had already begun to bring them into a place of rest. For inasmuch as the two tribes and a half had here chosen their home, they might behold as in a mirror that the possession of the promised land awaited them. Hence, then, Moses concludes that they were under obligation to keep the law, and exhorts them to shew their gratitude by faithful and sincere obedience. The object, therefore, of the recital is, to procure reverent attention to his doctrine; since the word שכל,
תשכילו; A. V., that ye may prosper. S.M., ut prudenter agatis; but he adds, the Hebrews, explain this word by הצליחו, “that ye may prosper.” The Hiphil of שכל, says Simon’s Lexicon, is to act prudently, and by a metonymy of the antecedent for the consequent, to proceed prosperously. — W.
shakal, in Hiphil, means to act successfully as well as prudently. I have set down both readings, since they are alike suitable to the sense. For we have seen in chapter 4, that this was the people’s only wisdom to obey God’s statutes; nor was their prosperity to be expected from any other source except God’s blessing, which is everywhere promised to the Israelites, if they keep the law.

Deuteronomy 11:10-12
